VIDEO.title: They Were Closest to Jesus — And Still Missed What God Was Doing
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 26:3-16 · Episode 50 (#53 of 58 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 26:3-16. The chief priests and elders meet in the court of Caiaphas and plot to seize Jesus by stealth, but not during the festival. In Bethany, at the home of Simon the leper, a woman pours an alabaster jar of very costly perfume on Jesus' head. The disciples are indignant: 'Why this waste?' Jesus defends her: she has prepared Him for burial, and she will be remembered wherever the gospel is proclaimed. Then Judas goes to the chief priests, and they weigh out thirty pieces of silver.

Jesus is surrounded by adversaries: the leaders plotting (26:3-5), His own disciples opposing what He affirms (26:6-9), and Judas plotting with the chief priests (26:14-16). John identifies the woman as Mary of Bethany and says Judas objected (John 12:3-5).

Messiah means anointed one. Kings (Saul, David, Solomon, Joash, Jehu) and priests were anointed, and so were the tabernacle and its furnishings (Exodus 30:22-30). Oil also meant joy: 'the oil of joy' (Psalm 45:7) and 'the oil of rejoicing instead of mourning' (Isaiah 61:3). The disciples should have recognized the symbolism.

Thirty pieces of silver was the price of a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32) and the insulting wage Israel paid the prophet in Zechariah 11:12-13, which he threw 'to the potter in the house of Yahweh.' Judas will throw the silver into the sanctuary, and it will buy the Potter's Field (27:3-10). The plot echoes Psalm 31:13: 'They schemed to take my life.'

The lesson: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God. Like the Pharisees in Matthew 12:7, the disciples condemned the innocent. They should have let Jesus' reaction guide theirs.
QUOTES: Lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God.
The disciples should have recognized this symbolic act for what it was.
They heard Jesus speak of his death, but they had no category for a Messiah whose kingship would come through atoning suffering.
They should have let Jesus reaction guide their response.

method.p: When something in a passage puzzles you, look first at how Jesus reacts to it, and let His response shape yours.

PLOT.title: Plotting in the court of Caiaphas

src.text: Then the chief priests and the elders of the people were gathered together in the court of the high priest, named Caiaphas; and they plotted together to seize Jesus by stealth and kill Him. But they were saying, “Not during the festival, lest a riot occur among the people.”

lines.text: Jesus is surrounded by adversaries: the leaders plot His murder, His disciples oppose what He affirms, and one of them plots to betray Him.

PLOT.title: They schemed to take my life

left.text: For I have heard the bad report of many, / Terror is on every side; / While they took counsel together against me, / They schemed to take my life.

right.text: Into Your hand I commit my spirit; / You have ransomed me, O Yahweh, God of truth.

lines.text: David takes refuge in the Lord while surrounded by enemies. Jesus quotes verse 5 with His last breath (Luke 23:46), and the leaders' plotting matches verse 13.

src.text: a woman came to Him with an alabaster jar of very costly perfume, and she poured it on His head as He reclined at the table. But when the disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste? For this perfume might have been sold for a high price and the money given to the poor.”

lines.text: John names the woman as Mary of Bethany, Martha's sister, and says Judas objected (John 12:3-5). In Matthew the objection spreads to the rest of the disciples; Mark says 'they were scolding her' (Mark 14:5).
The disciples cared more about what the oil could have bought than what it was accomplishing.

ANOINT.title: Anointed like a king and priest

left.text: And you shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and you shall set them apart as holy, that they may minister as priests to Me.

right.text: You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; / Therefore God, Your God, has anointed You / With the oil of joy above Your companions.

lines.text: Messiah means anointed one. Saul, David, Solomon, Joash and Jehu were anointed as kings (1 Samuel 16; 2 Samuel 2; 1 Kings 1; 2 Kings 9), and the holy anointing oil set apart the tent of meeting, the ark, the lampstand, the altars and the priests.
The video compares it to someone standing in front of the US Capitol and reciting the presidential oath of office.

src.text: To grant those who mourn in Zion, / Giving them a headdress instead of ashes, / The oil of rejoicing instead of mourning, / The mantle of praise instead of a spirit of fainting. / So they will be called oaks of righteousness, / The planting of Yahweh, that He may show forth His beautiful glory.

lines.text: Whether or not she grasped all its depth, her act resonates with Isaiah 61: joy, anointing and messianic fulfillment. It says Jesus is king, priest, and about to be buried.
Jesus was right: 'what this woman has done will also be spoken of in memory of her' (26:13). Paul uses the same fragrance imagery: 'we are a fragrance of Christ to God' (2 Corinthians 2:15).

left.text: and said, “What are you willing to give me to deliver Him to you?” And they weighed out thirty pieces of silver to him.

right.text: If the ox gores a male or female slave, the owner shall give his or her master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.

lines.text: Thirty pieces of silver was a low amount that represented the value of a slave's life. The chief priests may be showing they see Jesus as no more than a lowly slave, or as compensation for property damage.
How did Judas know which group to go to? We're not told.

left.text: Then Yahweh said to me, “Throw it to the potter, that valuable price at which I was valued by them.” So I took the thirty shekels of silver and threw them to the potter in the house of Yahweh.

right.text: And he threw the pieces of silver into the sanctuary and departed; and he went away and hanged himself.

lines.text: The people sarcastically valued the prophet at a slave's price; God called them the unworthy ones. Judas will throw the silver into the sanctuary, and it will buy the Potter's Field (27:7).
Matthew 27:9 credits the fulfillment to 'Jeremiah the prophet'; the wording draws on Zechariah 11:12-13 with echoes of Jeremiah 18-19 and 32.

src.text: But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire compassion, and not a sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent.

lines.text: When the hungry disciples plucked grain on the Sabbath, the Pharisees condemned them. Now the disciples condemn the woman: they have not learned the lesson.
Jesus neither stops nor scolds her. That should have been their clue; if they had questions, they could have asked Him privately later.

BACKGROUND.p: Costly perfumes were imported and kept sealed in alabaster flasks. Mark and John value this one at about three hundred denarii, roughly a year's wages (Mark 14:5; John 12:5). Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.
A village on the far slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem, where Jesus stayed during Passover week (21:17).
Joseph Caiaphas served as high priest about AD 18-36, the longest tenure of the period. An ossuary inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas' was found in Jerusalem in 1990.

DEBATES.p: Matthew, Mark and John describe an anointing at Bethany; Luke 7:36-50 tells of a sinful woman in Galilee. Most see Matthew, Mark and John as one event and Luke's as different.
The video asks whether she deliberately enacted Isaiah 61. Others think Jesus gave her act a meaning she may not have fully grasped. The video leaves it open.
Matthew 27:9 names Jeremiah. Explanations include a combined quotation (Zechariah 11 with Jeremiah 18-19 and 32) or citing the better-known prophet.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: John names the woman in John 12:3; John 12:7 is Jesus' reply.
The 'oil' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 is verse 24 (Asher dipping his foot in oil); 33:4 is about the law.
John says Judas objected; that he objected 'first' and the others followed is the video's inference.
John places the anointing six days before the Passover (John 12:1); Matthew tells it after the 'two days' note (26:2) without dating it.
That the perfume's scent lingered for days, reaching Pilate and the soldiers, is the video's imaginative picture, not stated in the text.

QUESTIONS: Why did the disciples see waste where Jesus saw a good work?
What does anointing mean for kings, priests and holy things?
How do Exodus 21 and Zechariah 11 shape the meaning of thirty pieces of silver?
Where might a lack of mercy be keeping you from seeing what God is doing?
How can you let Jesus' response guide yours when you don't understand?
In what ways are you 'a fragrance of Christ' where you live?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God. The disciples looked with the wrong eyes; they should have let Jesus' reaction guide their response and shown the woman mercy even when they could not understand. The video asks: is there a disagreement, perhaps with a brother or sister over secondary theology, where a lack of mercy is keeping you from seeing God at work?
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): think of one person whose devotion you have criticized. Ask what Jesus might see in it, and offer them a word of mercy this week.

## The plot
1. Matthew 26:3-5: Plotting in the court of Caiaphas
   By stealth Matthew 26:3-5: "Then the chief priests and the elders of the people were gathered together in the court of the high priest, named Caiaphas; and they plotted together to seize Jesus by stealth and kill Him. But they were saying, “Not during the festival, lest a riot occur among the people.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+26:3-5
   (video) Jesus is surrounded by adversaries: the leaders plot His murder, His disciples oppose what He affirms, and one of them plots to betray Him.
2. Psalm 31:5, 13: They schemed to take my life
   David (Psalm 31:13, LSB): "For I have heard the bad report of many, / Terror is on every side; / While they took counsel together against me, / They schemed to take my life."
   David (Psalm 31:5, LSB): "Into Your hand I commit my spirit; / You have ransomed me, O Yahweh, God of truth."

## Key people
- Caiaphas: The high priest in whose court the leaders plot. [Background] High priest c. AD 18-36, son-in-law of Annas (John 18:13).
- The woman (Mary of Bethany): Anoints Jesus' head; John names her Mary, Martha's sister. [Background] In John she anoints His feet and wipes them with her hair (John 12:3).
- Simon the leper: Host of the meal in Bethany. [Background] Otherwise unknown; perhaps healed by Jesus.
- Judas Iscariot: Goes to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. [Background] John calls him a thief who kept the money box (John 12:6).
- Zechariah the prophet: Valued at a slave's price; throws the silver to the potter. [Background] Prophet after the exile, c. 520 BC.

## Places [Background]
- Bethany (named in the video): The home of Simon the leper, where Jesus was anointed (26:6).
- Temple: Judas will throw the silver into the sanctuary (27:5).
- Court of Caiaphas (traditional) (named in the video): The leaders plot in the high priest's court (26:3); traditionally placed in the Upper City.

## Key terms
- Messiah: 'Anointed one': the anointed king (Greek Christos).
- Anointing: Pouring oil to set apart kings, priests and holy things; also a sign of joy.
- Alabaster jar: A sealed stone flask for costly perfume. [Background]
- Thirty pieces of silver: The price of a slave (Exodus 21:32) and Zechariah's insulting wage.
- Potter's Field: The field bought with Judas's silver, the Field of Blood (27:7-8).

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Perfume and burial: Costly perfumes were imported and kept sealed in alabaster flasks. Mark and John value this one at about three hundred denarii, roughly a year's wages (Mark 14:5; John 12:5). Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.
- Bethany: A village on the far slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem, where Jesus stayed during Passover week (21:17).
- Caiaphas: Joseph Caiaphas served as high priest about AD 18-36, the longest tenure of the period. An ossuary inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas' was found in Jerusalem in 1990.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For Jacob too anointed a pillar to God, and oil was offered in the sacrifices, and the priests were anointed with ointment." Homilies on Matthew 80, on 26:6-13. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For saying, that it might have been sold for three hundred pence, they showed how much this woman had spent on the ointment, and how great generosity she had manifested." Homilies on Matthew 80, on 26:9. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- One anointing or more? Matthew, Mark and John describe an anointing at Bethany; Luke 7:36-50 tells of a sinful woman in Galilee. Most see Matthew, Mark and John as one event and Luke's as different.
- Did Mary know? The video asks whether she deliberately enacted Isaiah 61. Others think Jesus gave her act a meaning she may not have fully grasped. The video leaves it open.
- Jeremiah or Zechariah? Matthew 27:9 names Jeremiah. Explanations include a combined quotation (Zechariah 11 with Jeremiah 18-19 and 32) or citing the better-known prophet.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- John names the woman in John 12:3; John 12:7 is Jesus' reply.
- The 'oil' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 is verse 24 (Asher dipping his foot in oil); 33:4 is about the law.
- John says Judas objected; that he objected 'first' and the others followed is the video's inference.
- John places the anointing six days before the Passover (John 12:1); Matthew tells it after the 'two days' note (26:2) without dating it.
- That the perfume's scent lingered for days, reaching Pilate and the soldiers, is the video's imaginative picture, not stated in the text.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why did the disciples see waste where Jesus saw a good work?
2. What does anointing mean for kings, priests and holy things?
3. How do Exodus 21 and Zechariah 11 shape the meaning of thirty pieces of silver?
4. Where might a lack of mercy be keeping you from seeing what God is doing?
5. How can you let Jesus' response guide yours when you don't understand?
6. In what ways are you 'a fragrance of Christ' where you live?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God. The disciples looked with the wrong eyes; they should have let Jesus' reaction guide their response and shown the woman mercy even when they could not understand. The video asks: is there a disagreement, perhaps with a brother or sister over secondary theology, where a lack of mercy is keeping you from seeing God at work?
- Study note (added): think of one person whose devotion you have criticized. Ask what Jesus might see in it, and offer them a word of mercy this week.
